stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the 1970s, many North American cities were widening downtown streets so that cars could move through them faster. Dutch urban planner ______ the opposite: in a series of pilot projects in Rotterdam, she narrowed traffic lanes, planted trees along the curbs, and demonstrated that slower traffic brought more pedestrians, and more business, to the street.
explanation: There is no 'the' or 'a' in front of 'Dutch urban planner,' so the title and the name work together as one label for the subject. The name is essential, so it takes no commas, and nothing should separate the subject 'Marieke Hoorn' from its verb 'argued.'

B.why: You put a single comma between the subject 'Marieke Hoorn' and its verb 'argued.' A lone comma should never split a subject from its verb.

C.why: You treated the name as an appositive, as in 'my friend, Ana, said.' Without an article before the title, the name is essential to the noun phrase, so a pair of commas around it is wrong.

D.why: You put a colon after 'Dutch urban planner,' which is not a complete sentence. A colon needs a complete sentence on its left, and here it also cuts the title off from the name it labels.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Decades before mRNA vaccines reached clinics, the idea that the immune system could be trained to tolerate a substance rather than attack it had few champions. Canadian immunologist ______ one of them; her 1984 experiments in mice showed that repeated low doses of an allergen could quiet, rather than provoke, an inflammatory response.
explanation: 'Canadian immunologist' has no article in front of it, so it acts as a title attached directly to the name. The whole phrase 'Canadian immunologist Ruth Okafor-Lind' is the subject. Leave out all punctuation between the title and the name and between the name and the verb 'was.'

A.why: You set the name off with appositive commas. Those commas only work when an article such as 'a' or 'the' comes before the title. Here the name is essential and can't be fenced off.

B.why: You put a comma between the subject 'Ruth Okafor-Lind' and the verb 'was,' which splits the subject from its verb.

D.why: A pair of dashes does the same job as a pair of commas: it fences off a removable interruption. The name isn't removable here, so the dashes are wrong for the same reason paired commas would be.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: After a 1999 swarm of small earthquakes beneath an ice cap in southeastern Iceland, most researchers assumed the tremors were volcanic in origin. Icelandic seismologist ______ a different explanation: the melting ice, by removing weight from the crust beneath it, was allowing long-dormant faults to slip.
explanation: No article comes before 'Icelandic seismologist,' so the title and name form a single noun phrase that serves as the subject. It takes no punctuation inside it and no comma before the verb 'proposed.'

A.why: You placed a comma after the name, which separates the subject from its verb 'proposed.'

C.why: You placed a comma between the title and the name, as if the name were a nonessential appositive. Without an article, the title and the name belong together and can't be separated.

D.why: You used a colon after 'Icelandic seismologist,' which is a fragment. You also added a comma that splits the subject from the verb. Both marks are misplaced.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Drawing on dietary records from more than 40,000 adults in eleven countries, some of them kept for over two decades, Australian nutrition scientist ______ that people who ate beans, lentils, or other legumes daily lived measurably longer than those who rarely ate them, even after accounting for income and smoking.
explanation: The long opening modifier already ends with the comma after 'decades.' The main clause starts with 'Australian nutrition scientist,' which has no article, so the title and name work as one subject. No punctuation belongs between the title and the name, or between the name and 'concluded.'

A.why: The long introductory phrase made you feel another break was needed, so you put a comma between the title and the name. The intro already ended at 'decades,' and the title and name can't be separated.

B.why: You put a comma after the name, which splits the subject 'Priya Venkataraman' from its verb 'concluded.'

C.why: You used appositive commas around the name. Without 'a' or 'the' before the title, the name is essential and takes no commas.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the early days of weather radar, faint echoes that forecasters nicknamed "angels" were routinely dismissed as instrument noise. British meteorologist ______ that the mysterious returns were in fact flocks of migrating birds and swarms of insects carried aloft by rising warm air, a finding that eventually made radar as useful to ecologists as to forecasters.
explanation: 'British meteorologist' has no article before it, so it works as a title attached directly to the name. The full subject is 'British meteorologist Edwin Marchbanks,' and it flows straight into the verb 'showed' with no punctuation.

A.why: You put a comma between the subject and its verb 'showed.' A single comma can't split a subject from its verb.

C.why: You put a comma between the title and the name, as if the name were an appositive. With no article in front of the title, the name is essential and stays attached.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so it needs a complete sentence before it. 'British meteorologist' is a fragment, and the dash cuts the title off from the name.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The fossil leaves at the center of the debate—collected in 2011 by Argentine paleobotanist ______ ash beds in Patagonia—preserve tiny crescent-shaped bite marks. Their shapes suggest that leaf-eating insects recovered far more quickly from the asteroid impact that ended the Cretaceous than researchers had believed.
explanation: Inside the dash-enclosed interruption, 'Argentine paleobotanist' has no article, so the title and name form one phrase that is the object of 'by.' Nothing should separate the title from the name or the name from 'from ash beds.' The closing dash after 'Patagonia' already finishes the interruption.

B.why: You added a comma after the name, cutting 'from ash beds' off from the phrase 'collected ... by Argentine paleobotanist Lucía Ferrante.' That comma breaks up the interruption for no grammatical reason.

C.why: You treated the name as a nonessential appositive. Without 'a' or 'the' before the title, the name is essential, so commas around it are wrong.

D.why: You put a single comma between the title and the name, splitting a phrase that has to stay together because no article comes before the title.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When sea otters recolonized a coastal slough in central California in the 1980s, few biologists expected them to help the estuary's struggling eelgrass. Yet marine ecologist ______ a clear chain of effects: the otters ate crabs, fewer crabs meant more sea slugs, and the slugs grazed away the algae that had been smothering the grass.
explanation: 'Marine ecologist' has no article in front of it, so the title and name together form the subject. The subject runs directly into the verb 'traced,' with no comma between the title and the name and none after the name.

A.why: You put a comma after the name, which separates the subject from its verb 'traced.'

B.why: You remembered the appositive pattern ('a scientist, Dolores, said') and used it here. With no article before the title, the name is essential and can't be set off with commas.

C.why: You put a colon after 'Yet marine ecologist Dolores Nakamura-Reyes,' which is not a complete sentence. The colon also splits the subject from its verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: For decades, coaches told distance runners to hold long static stretches before every race. Norwegian sports scientist ______ that advice to the test in 2009. She timed 300 competitive runners over five kilometers after either static stretching or a light jog; the runners who had stretched finished, on average, slightly slower.
explanation: No 'a' or 'the' comes before 'Norwegian sports scientist,' so the title and name act as one label and form the subject together. Use no punctuation between the title and the name, or between the name and the verb 'put.'

A.why: You put a comma between the title and the name. Without an article, the title and name are a single noun phrase and can't be separated.

B.why: You put a comma after the name, which splits the subject 'Sigrid Aalvik' from its verb 'put.'

D.why: You set the name off with a pair of appositive commas. That only works when an article comes before the title. Here the name is essential.
